title: CAFE: Closed-Loop Autonomous Task Formulation and Execution without Instance-Specific Instructions
why: A-type scene-driven household-robot harness: an online memory of objects, functional zones, and execution states feeds a rule-guided Trigger-LLM plus Draft/Complete/Audit LLMs that formulate, detail, and dependency-check tasks under predefined cleaning, safety, and storage categories, without instance-specific goals; outcomes update memory for correction and later discovery.
mechanism: CAFE keeps an online memory of objects, functional zones, and execution states. A rule-guided Trigger-LLM admits task formulation from accumulated evidence; Draft, Complete, and Audit propose goals, resolve execution details, and check dependencies. Execution outcomes write back into memory for correction and subsequent discovery. Tasks are drawn from predefined cleaning, safety, and storage/organization categories rather than instance-specific instructions.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): evaluation in 12 AI2-THOR scenes compares three backbones and task-complexity tiers using coverage, constraint, and execution metrics. A Tri-LLM variant records higher GCR scores than the evaluated baselines across those backbones and tiers. Controls examine completion, auditing, zones, feedback, triggering, and prompt examples. LimoCobot traces illustrate storage, cleanup, and recovery from a failed grasp. Numeric tables beyond the abstract unread.

title: RoboACE: Adversarial Co-Evolution for Robot Self-Improvement
why: A-type embodied self-improvement loop that jointly evolves a curriculum harness and an execution harness around frozen foundation models, so practice selection and reusable skill/planning/recovery revisions co-adapt from execution feedback.
mechanism: RoboACE (Robot Adversarial Co-Evolution) jointly evolves curriculum and execution harnesses around frozen foundation models. The curriculum harness uses accumulated capability evidence to propose informative challenges; the execution harness responds with reusable revisions that expand skills, planning procedures, and recovery strategies. Alternating updates hold one side fixed while the other changes, and admitted challenges form fixed snapshots for comparing execution revisions. After practice starting from a compact set of LIBERO conditions, the resulting frozen deployment is evaluated against controllers and agent systems.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): the frozen deployment outperforms the evaluated controllers and agent systems across four LIBERO-family panels. On LIBERO-PRO it reaches 74.0% success, 15.0 points above the initial deployment and 13.5 points above direct execution by its VLA controller. Case studies document changes to evidence-guided practice selection, drawer-skill grounding, and controller intervention. Numeric tables beyond the abstract unread.

title: Robo-MLT: Dual-System Robotic Manipulation for Long-Horizon Medical Laboratory Tasks
why: A-type dual-system lab-manipulation harness: a vision-language planner composes an ordered atomic-skill sequence, a multiframe execution monitor advances the workflow or triggers replanning when a skill completes or becomes infeasible, and a skill-conditioned VLA generates trajectories under an asynchronous runtime.
mechanism: Robo-MLT couples explicit workflow monitoring with learned action generation. A vision-language planner composes an ordered atomic-skill sequence from the protocol and the initial workspace observation. A multiframe execution monitor detects when the active skill has completed or become infeasible, then advances the workflow or triggers replanning. A skill-conditioned vision-language-action policy generates the manipulation trajectories, and an asynchronous runtime coordinates the policy with the monitor.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): evaluated against four policy baselines and a VLM-based monitor baseline on blood gas analysis and blood sample tube sorting, with 50 nominal configurations per method and 20 sample-removal configurations. Robo-MLT achieves task success rates of 82% and 70%, exceeding π0.5 by 30 and 22 percentage points, respectively. After an operator removes the sample being handled, the system revises the remaining plan and continues processing the other samples. Numeric tables beyond the abstract unread.

title: LEASH: Stay Safe in Agentic Robotics
why: B-type closed-loop safety benchmark (RoboRisk) plus an A-type lease-enforced safety harness (LEASH) with shared-policy task, action, and commit gates for foundation-model agentic robot control, evaluated in simulation and on physical robots.
mechanism: RoboRisk is a closed-loop safety benchmark for agentic robotics with 92 simulated tasks and 13 physical-robot tasks in five categories: Task-level Refusal, Plan Repair, Execution-time Hazard, Injection, and Sequential Memory. LEASH (Lease-Enforced Agentic Safety Harness) is intended to integrate into nearly any agentic architecture: a decision model (Jev or OpenAI's Decisions API) implements task, action, and commit gates that review the task, each action, and each irreversible operation in their visual context. The planner and all three gates share a common safety policy.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): six foundation models (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, and Grok 4.7) generally show high harm rates on RoboRisk; two robot-specific APIs (Dream API and PokeBot's RoboAPI) are also evaluated. Experiments in simulation and on physical robots report that LEASH reduces harm across all six foundation models, largely preserves task-completion performance, and adds little time and token overhead. Numeric tables beyond the abstract unread.

title: Is Your Robot's Memory Just a Clock? Temporal Shortcuts in Memory-Augmented VLA Policies
why: B-type audit of memory-augmented VLA policies: time-sampled, time-stamped memory confuses waiting with work (phantom progress), and the paper contrasts clock-indexed memory with event-indexed memory as a harness-level fix.
mechanism: The paper tests memory-augmented VLA policies whose memory is filled by uniformly sampling frames and stamping each with its time step. On RoboMME counting tasks, a brief pause or wrist fidget (a null event) is counted as work, producing early stopping termed phantom progress. Withholding the same frames from memory restores success, locating the failure in memory rather than in the interruption. Rescaling time stamps alone makes the policy stop early when the clock runs fast and repeat when it runs slow. Removing the time encoding does not cure the failure, because null-event frames still occupy slots of the time-sampled memory. Training with injected pauses does not remove the failure and impairs counting, whereas indexing memory by events recovers half or more of the loss without retraining.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): on RoboMME counting tasks, the null-event intervention cuts success from 47 to 16 of 50 on one task and from 44 to 10 on the other. When the same frames are withheld from memory, success returns. Across RoboMME's released designs, vulnerability follows how memory is indexed. Event-indexed memory recovers half or more of the loss without retraining. Numeric tables and other tasks beyond the abstract unread.

title: Cognitive Multi-Agent Search and Rescue: Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Collaborative Robotics
why: A-type language-grounded multi-robot harness for search and rescue: an LLM interprets human instructions into semantic cues that guide hierarchical strategy selection and role assignment across UAV and UGV agents that share a cognitive workspace.
mechanism: A Cognitive Multi-Agent Framework based on Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (LG-HRL) integrates natural-language understanding, hierarchical policy decomposition, and a shared cognitive workspace. Human instructions are interpreted by an LLM and transformed into structured semantic cues that guide high-level strategy selection and role assignment across UAV and UGV agents. The authors introduce a Language-Grounded Multi-Agent Hierarchical Decision Process (LG-MAHDP) to model the interplay between semantic grounding, hierarchical control, and distributed coordination.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): in a simulated disaster environment, LG-HRL improves learning speed by 2.3 times, increases coordination coherence by 37%, and enhances subgoal accuracy and hazard avoidance by 46% and 31%, respectively. The system achieves 20-30% higher victim rescue rates, demonstrates emergent role specialization, and adapts immediately to human verbal updates. Ablation studies report that both the shared cognitive workspace and language grounding are critical. Numeric tables beyond the abstract unread.

title: Embodied Science Agents: Making Embodied Experimental Design Learnable
why: A-type self-driving-lab harness that couples a memory-and-Bayesian-optimisation digital agent with an embodied agent for generalisable instrument control through a unified interface, closing the loop between experimental reasoning and physical action.
mechanism: The paper argues that self-driving laboratories often treat foundation models as disembodied planners that output symbolic workflows for separate robots, blocking embodied experimental intuition. It proposes learnability along three axes (cognitive, experimental, and embodied) and introduces the Embodied Science Agent (ESA): a Digital Agent providing memory-based reasoning and Bayesian optimisation, an Embodied Agent providing generalisable instrument control, and an Embodied Unified Interface for coordination. Learned visuomotor policies are reported to generalise across varying instrument placements.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): ESA was validated in autonomous wastewater treatment experiments, navigating over 200 million possible conditions. Through 15 continuous rounds, ESA raised the final solution transmittance from 82% to 99.7%, described as a 98.5% reduction in residual dye concentration and near-complete decolourisation, while learned visuomotor policies generalised across varying instrument placements. Numeric tables beyond the abstract unread.

title: A Comprehensive Survey of Agent Distillation across Models, Artifacts, and Harnesses
why: Update of the known agent-distillation survey already in the corpus: v2 retitles the paper and substantially rewrites the framing into a unified Agent Distillation survey with a knowledge-substrate taxonomy (models, artifacts, or harnesses), cross-substrate transfer paths, and evaluation protocols for retention, causal attribution, and deployed utility.
mechanism: v1 was titled 'Distilling Agentic Systems: A Roadmap across Models, Artifacts, and Harnesses' and organised the field by where transferred knowledge is retained (within the model, as artifacts, through the execution harness, or across substrates). v2 retitles the work as a comprehensive survey, formalizes Agent Distillation as persistent knowledge transfer between teacher and student agents, distinguishes experience used for transfer from knowledge retained for reuse, develops a knowledge-substrate taxonomy (models, artifacts, or harnesses), and analyses cross-substrate transfer paths and hybrid strategies, plus benchmarks and evaluation protocols for retention, causal attribution, and deployed utility without further teacher support.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (v2 abstract): this is a survey formalization and literature review rather than a new closed-loop robot experiment. Comments change from 57 pages, 5 figures (v1) to 35 pages, 6 figures (v2). Full-text comparison unread.
